      <description><p>Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result</p><p>The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.</p><p>Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994.       <description><p>Party expected to get less than a third of the vote amid frustration over water outages and power cuts</p><p>The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure.</p><p>The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. News from the US, Europe, Asia Pacific, Africa, Middle East, America</description><link>https://www.france24.com/en/</link><lastBuildDate>Sun, 08 Nov 2026 12:23:51 GMT</lastBuildDate><atom:link href="https://www.france24.com/en/rss" rel="self" type="application/rss+xml"/><item><category>France</category><title>‘10 times more painful’: Menstrual disorders fuel calls to ban tear gas at French protests</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261108-abnormal-menstraution-periods-fuel-calls-ban-tear-gas-french-protests-police</link><description>
French police have made extensive use of tear gas during protests that have roiled France in recent weeks, sometimes causing grievous injuries. Thousands of accounts of women experiencing acutely painful periods and increased bleeding are further challenging assumptions that the chemical irritant carries only minor consequences.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/a664e012-da11-11f1-ab05-695cb59fade5/w:1024/p:16x9/000-D3LF967.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/a664e012-da11-11f1-ab05-695cb59fade5/w:1024/p:16x9/000-D3LF967.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">e3240f6a-d9fc-11f1-ac74-9777b0a3a97d</guid><pubDate>Sun, 08 Nov 2026 11:53:14 GMT</pubDate><source url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/a664e012-da11-11f1-ab05-695cb59fade5/w:1024/p:16x9/000-D3LF967.jpg">© Ed Jones, AFP</source><dc:creator>Benjamin DODMAN</dc:creator></item><item><category>Sports</category><title>2026 Dakar Youth Olympic Games: Golden Double for Senegal</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/sports/20261108-2026-dakar-youth-olympic-games-golden-double-for-senegal</link><description>
Senegal won two gold medals in beach wrestling at the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar. Elisabeth Diatta won gold in the -55 kg category, the host country’s first gold medal at the Youth Olympic Games. Her compatriot Maguette Diop followed suit, taking gold in the -80 kg category.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/ed16cfe6-db62-11f1-971d-a575454bc579/w:1024/p:16x9/JOJ-DAKAR-2026.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/ed16cfe6-db62-11f1-971d-a575454bc579/w:1024/p:16x9/JOJ-DAKAR-2026.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">48704b16-db35-11f1-84de-35ca72a4bcea</guid><pubDate>Sun, 08 Nov 2026 10:56:56 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE 24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>Diwali: Over one billion people mark victory of light over darkness</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/diwali-over-one-billion-people-mark-victory-of-light-over-darkness</link><description>
Diwali celebrations began on Sunday, with people across India and the global diaspora gathering to mark one of the most important festivals in the Hindu tradition. In Ayodhya, believed to be the birthplace of Lord Rama, the deity celebrated during the festival, festivities included performances based on the Hindu epic Ramayana, laser and light shows, live music, fireworks and drone displays.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/cac0a34c-db60-11f1-b422-a575454bc579/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261108-111252-111423-CS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/cac0a34c-db60-11f1-b422-a575454bc579/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261108-111252-111423-CS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">cfba9c7c-db60-11f1-9841-59074deecd2b</guid><pubDate>Sun, 08 Nov 2026 10:46:37 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>Paraguay: Senate impeached Peña rather than accept his offer to resign</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261108-paraguay-senate-impeached-pe%C3%B1a-rather-than-accept-his-offer-to-resign</link><description>
Paraguay's ousted president, Santiago Peña, has been charged over the collapse of Ueno Bank. Initially placed under house arrest, he has since been transferred to a military facility for his own safety. Nearly three million customers were locked out of their accounts after regulators seized control of the online bank. Repayments are now under way, but protests continue as customers demand access to their money. Peña denies any wrongdoing. Jack Pownall reports.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/97992746-db60-11f1-b875-695cb59fade5/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261108-111033-111218-CS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/97992746-db60-11f1-b875-695cb59fade5/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261108-111033-111218-CS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">9c89fc9e-db60-11f1-b55f-b7e2ef7616a9</guid><pubDate>Sun, 08 Nov 2026 10:42:59 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category>Middle East</category><title>Middle East live: Riyadh's financial district targeted following deadly Saudi strikes in Yemen</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/20261108-middle-east-live-riyadh-financial-district-targeted-deadly-strikes-yemen-israel-eisenkot-netanyahu-coalition-government-elections</link><description>
Riyadh’s Aramco Tower was damaged by falling debris on Sunday after the Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthi rebels intercepted two ballistic missiles headed for the capital’s financial district. The attack comes a day after Saudi ​air strikes killed at least 33 people near Sanaa. Follow our liveblog for the latest developments from the Middle East.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/0e783f10-db4c-11f1-abfd-a575454bc579/w:1024/p:16x9/7f554331a6cdd64418e7973b0fb73c45bab02694.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/0e783f10-db4c-11f1-abfd-a575454bc579/w:1024/p:16x9/7f554331a6cdd64418e7973b0fb73c45bab02694.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">4f9136bc-db58-11f1-b6e9-1d122f9c1034</guid><pubDate>Sun, 08 Nov 2026 09:47:36 GMT</pubDate><source url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/0e783f10-db4c-11f1-abfd-a575454bc579/w:1024/p:16x9/7f554331a6cdd64418e7973b0fb73c45bab02694.jpg">© Fayez Nureldine, AFP</source><dc:creator>Louise NORDSTROM</dc:creator></item></channel></rss>

<![CDATA[ Latest from Space.com ]]> https://www.space.com/feeds.xml Sun, 08 Nov 2026 11:00:00 +0000 en <![CDATA[ Scientists simulate an Earth without life to help hunt for aliens and inhabited worlds ]]> A new computer simulation that depicts Earth, or a rocky planet in general, without life is the latest tool in the quest to discover whether or not we are alone in the universe.

Life leaves its mark on a planet, particularly its atmosphere, in the form of a mixture of biochemically created gases. Some are obvious, while others can be produced by both biology and geology, meaning that distinguishing a planet that has life from one that does not, solely based on what gases we can detect in its atmosphere, can be difficult. The key is in knowing which atmospheric conditions can be explained without life.

To aid in distinguishing between habitable and inhabited planets, planetary scientist Samantha Gilbert-Janizek of the University of California, Riverside, developed a model that simulates the evolution of a rocky planet without life.

"The model can help us see how habitable but non-living planets might mimic living planets," Gilbert-Janizek, who was a PhD student at the University of Washington when the research was conducted, said in a statement.

Gilbert-Janizek built upon a model previously developed by Washington’s Rory Barnes that simulated the core, mantle, and crust of a planet. This new model pushed the simulation two steps further by incorporating the surface and atmosphere of the planet as well.

In all, the model simulates 19 properties of a rocky planet that are not related to life, including the amount of heat a planet receives from its star, the exchange of heat and chemicals from the core to the surface, and the outflow of certain gases from the subsurface.

Gilbert-Janizek’s starting point was to simulate the development of Earth had life never arisen here, therefore providing a baseline with which to compare to exoplanets. She ran the simulation from the birth of Earth 4.5 billion years ago to 500 million years into the future. The result was a lifeless world, but one that still had oceans and an atmosphere.

"When we interpret observations of an exoplanet’s atmosphere, this tool will help us determine the probability that what we observe indicates life on the surface," said Gilbert-Janizek.

What makes the simulation especially useful is its plug-and-play nature. Researchers can simply apply the bulk properties of whichever planet they are studying to the model, and then just let it run. If the result is a planet with an atmosphere that matches what is detected spectroscopically by the James Webb Space Telescope or, in the future, the various extremely large 30-meter-plus ground-based telescopes or NASA’s planned Habitable Worlds Observatory, then we know that planet probably does not have life as we know it.

However, if the simulated planet without life does not match what we observe on the real planet, then it becomes possible that life is present and altering the atmosphere.

"Dr Gilbert-Janizek’s work represents an exciting step toward understanding where life can exist in the universe,” said Barnes. "After more than a decade of work by many scientists, Dr Gilbert-Janizek has finally completed a model of the Earth that simultaneously reproduces properties of Earth’s core, mantle, surface and atmosphere. That calibration gives us confidence that future simulations of exoplanets will be accurate."

While any deviation from what is predicted by the model will not necessarily mean there is definitely life on a planet, it will help pick out those worlds that are worthy of follow-up studies by the next generation of telescopes.

Gilbert-Janizek’s model is described in a paper published in The Planetary Science Journal.

]]> <![CDATA[ On this day in space! Nov. 7, 1992: NASA launches Mars Global Surveyor, its 1st Mars mission in 20 years at the time, to map the Red Planet like never before ]]>

On Nov. 7, 1996, NASA launched its Mars Global Surveyor mission. This was the first mission NASA sent to Mars in almost 20 years!

The Mars Global Surveyor spacecraft was an orbiter. It transmitted data from NASA's Mars rovers Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity back to Earth. The spacecraft also did a lot of its own science. It found surface channels on Mars that appeared to have been created by running water.

Mars Global Surveyor looked at the south pole of Mars and saw signs of possible climate change. It also saw a mineral called hematite on Mars. Hematite usually forms in water. NASA then sent its Spirit and Opportunity rovers to look for the hematite, and both rovers found it near their landing sites.

Mars Global Surveyor survived much longer than expected. But a space maneuver accidentally exposed one of its batteries to the sun, and the spacecraft lost power. It fell silent forever in November 2006.

Why it mattered

As the first successful Mars mission since the two Viking launches in 1975, Mars Global Surveyor ushered in a new era of exploration of the Red Planet, not only through its own contributions to orbit-based science, but by serving a relay for surface-based rovers. As such, it became a primary pipeline for multiple concurrent Mars missions.

"The [Mars Global Surveyor] mission overhauled scientists' understanding of Mars by studying the entire Martian surface, atmosphere and interior. Major findings included dramatic evidence that water still flows on Mars in short bursts down hillside gullies, and the identification of water-related mineral deposits leading to selection of a Mars rover landing site for a subsequent mission," read a NASA description of the probe.

Mars Global Surveyor sent back more than 240,000 images to Earth during its nine active years.

]]> <![CDATA[ Send your name to Saturn's moon Titan with NASA's upcoming Dragonfly mission ]]> We still may be some time away from sending humans to distant reaches of the solar system, but you can send your name to Saturn's moon Titan, which has the ingredients of life on its surface thanks to NASA's Dragonfly mission.

Dragonfly is an SUV-sized nuclear-powered rotorcraft that NASA aims to launch towards Titan in 2028. The agency opened a special events page in late October to allow members of the public to put their name on the spacecraft. The names will be put upon a chip on Dragonfly during the spacecraft's assembly, and all names must be submitted before Jan. 15, 2027.

The agency says that the mission has no "ordinary itinerary," as Dragonfly aims to between areas miles (or kilometers) apart after arriving on the surface in 2034. "Nearly a billion miles away, an extraordinary destination awaits. Titan has an atmosphere, rivers and lakes, seasons, sweeping dunes and a landscape rich in organic material," NASA officials wrote in the event page. "Upon arrival in 2034, Dragonfly will fly from place to place on this intriguing world to uncover clues about this remarkable moon, and the chemistry that could help us understand the ingredients for life."

Dragonfly will be one of just a few flying crafts on another world, with the first being NASA's plucky Ingenuity mini-helicopter that arrived on Mars along with the still-running Perseverance rover in 2021. Ingenuity was only designed to make five flights, but made it to 72 until its blades were damaged during a landing on Jan. 18, 2024.

NASA is now planning a SkyFall mission on Mars that would use three helicopters, and which may launch as soon as late 2028 for the Red Planet.

Dragonfly, however, is not the first mission to Titan: that would be Huygens, which operated for just a few hours on Jan. 14, 2005 after deploying from the Cassini spacecraft. Huygens was the first lander on an outer solar system world, and measured Titan's atmosphere and took data from the surface.

For its part, Cassini flew by Titan more than 100 times before the mission concluded in September 2017, providing valuable long-term data about the moon from above. Dragonfly aims to show the moon from up close for about 3.3 Earth years. Its destinations will include dunes and a young impact crater called Selk, according to NASA.

"Dragonfly is expected to make one flight every one to two Titan days, which is called a Tsol and lasts about 16 Earth days," NASA officials added of the mission. Dragonfly will stop at a variety of geologic sites, where it will collect samples of surface material for analysis inside the rotorcraft by a suite of scientific instruments."

Dragonfly's goals include learning more about prebiotic chemistry, or the conditions prior to life arising in a location; figuring out if Titan had habitable conditions in the past; and looking for "chemical indicators" of life based on water or hydrocarbons.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman is serious about launching "big rockets" to the moon every single year for the agency's Artemis program. And the new space race with China is fueling that ambition.

"I feel good. I feel like we are certainly on a more achievable path to the lunar surface today than where we were before," Isaacman told Space.com.

We recently sat down with the NASA chief to discuss the state of the Artemis program, and, off the bat, he made it clear that he's confident in the U.S. space program following the success of April's Artemis II mission around the moon. In fact, just prior to our conversation, it was announced that Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman will become the new deputy director of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. But the road from Artemis II's success to crewed lunar landings and, later, a permanent moon base will take a lot of launches of NASA's Space Launch System (SLS) megarocket, Isaacman stressed.

"You know, a lot of people, especially in the space community, start getting [into] if the landers are there or not. I don't really care about that right now. What I care about is that we are launching big rockets no less than once a year," he said.

"I think that's imperative for NASA to be doing these deep-space human spaceflight missions right now," Isaacman added. "So, we had a great mission in April of '26. We will launch again in '27."

That coming launch will be for Artemis III, a crewed mission to low Earth orbit that will test docking procedures between NASA's Orion capsule and one or both of the Artemis program's private lunar landers — SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon.

"We need to continue to exercise those muscles," he said, referring to SLS liftoffs. "And, honestly, once a year isn't great, either. I mean, I don't think we're going to get back to the early [space] shuttle days, you know, four missions a year. I don't think we're going to get back to where we were with Apollo, but once a year is the minimum … I would testify that to Congress in this role years down the road.

"If NASA is going to be doing deep-space missions, complicated missions, [we should] launch at least once a year and get as much out of it as you can for taking the risk and spending the taxpayer dollars and building towards something greater," Isaacman added. "That's what we're doing with Artemis III, and that's what's going to better prepare us for Artemis IV."

A new space race

So, how is NASA coping with the challenges that face them as they approach Artemis III ahead of a crewed lunar landing on Artemis IV, which is targeted for 2028? While NASA can learn some lessons from past moon missions with Apollo, today it's primarily relying on the extensive experience and talent within the agency, according to Isaacman.

"Artemis II is very different from Apollo 8, and Artemis III will be very different from Apollo 9," he said. "Our approach is not exactly the same as it was … But what is the same right now? The spirit, the energy, the potential within NASA. The talent of the workforce and industry is no different than the 1960s."

There's another similarity to the Apollo era: NASA has a rival in its race to the moon. While the adversary in the 1960s was the Soviet Union, today the U.S. is competing against China.

"It is a real space race," Isaacman said. But, he added, "this one is very different than the first one."

"Everything is closer than it was, not just in space. I mean, we had the edge in computing [and] every one of the technology domains during the Cold War. Our capabilities were better by a mile," he said. "[But with] China, it's not [like that]. They're very close."

"We're saying we're going to land on the moon at the end of 2028. China is saying by the end of 2029," Isaacman added. "And it's like, Well, are they going to pull it off? Yes, they will. They've showcased their landers, their rovers, their suits, two-launch architecture with built-in reusability."

So NASA is taking the Chinese threat very seriously, according to Isaacman.

"The consequence of getting this wrong, I'm telling you — it's going to be felt around the world," he said. "It will call everything into question."

"Should I be using American superintelligence or AI? Should I be doing Chinese? Should I be buying their computers? Should I be [buying] ours? Buying their cars, their airplanes, their ships? Whose security guarantees to trust?" Isaacman added. "I think the implications are pretty severe, which is why we're taking it so seriously and putting such extreme focus on the mission right now. But we have that playbook of success, and I think we will prevail."

]]> <![CDATA[ On this day in space! Nov. 6, 1572: A German astronomer discovers the Tycho supernova with the naked eye, but everyone thought the cosmic explosion was a 'new star' ]]>

On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova with his bare eyes. He spotted the exploding star in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day.

Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star."

At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago. Because Tycho's Star is 13,000 light-years from Earth, it took a while before anyone could see it.

Why it mattered

The Tycho supernova, known technically as SN 1572, is known today as a Type Ia supernova, which is a star explosion in a binary star system in which a white dwarf star draws material away from its partner, then explodes. But in 1572, the Tycho supernova appeared as something very different: a bright new star.

While Schulër was first, other astronomers also observed the apparently new star in the sky. Tycho Brahe's numerous observations are the most well known, in no small part becuause he wrote a book all about them in "De Stella Nova" (Latin for "On The New Star." At the time, the prevailing theory among scientists was that the stars were unchanging, yet here was a new star -- a changed sky.

"The 16th century exploding star, which appeared in the constellation Cassiopeia, was seen in daylight for about two weeks, and remained visible to the naked eye for 16 months," the University of California Berkeley wrote in 2004. "Brahe's meticulous record of the brightening and dimming of the supernova now allows astronomers to identify its 'light signature" as that of a Type Ia supernova."

"This was at the end of the Dark Ages in Europe, and these observations were an important piece of evidence that the heavens were not immutable," astronomer Alex Filippenko, who led a 2004 study on the origins of the Tycho supernova, said at the time.

Today, astronomers are closely watching another star that might explode. Called T Corona Borealis, or the Blaze Star, the object is expected to be on the verge of exploding in a nova (a star explosion that is smaller than a supernova and may not destroy the star). is one of 11 known stars observed to have recurring nova explosions within gaps of 100 years or so.

It's not a star at all! ]]> Early morning risers heading to work or school before sunrise are likely to notice a very bright, star-like object appearing low in the east-southeast sky just before sunrise. What is somewhat amazing is that just a couple of weeks ago this object wasn't there at all, but now it literally stands out with such brilliance as to almost command the attention of commuters who might be traveling in an easterly direction to "Look at me!"

The object in question is, of course, the planet Venus, which is currently amid one of its most spectacular forays into the morning sky, literally "vaulting up" into prominence.

On Oct. 24, Venus came to inferior conjunction, passing between the Earth and sun and shifting from the evening into the morning sky. And the view is only going to get better in the days and weeks to come!

Ascending in the morning

In terms of morning visibility, Venus is now in a literal and figurative sense "rising to the occasion." It's now rising before the break of dawn, more than 90 minutes before sunrise. From here on, it will rise three minutes earlier each day, so that by Dec. 17 it will rise 3 hours and 50 minutes before sunrise and blaze in a completely dark sky for more than two hours before the first vestige of morning twilight.

It will reach peak brilliance on Nov. 29, when it will shine at an eye-popping magnitude of -4.9. That's 12 times brighter than its nearest planetary competitor, Jupiter and a full 25 times more dazzling than Sirius, the brightest of all stars. If you live in a rural location with no light pollution to interfere, you might be able to make out that it is casting a visible shadow and if you follow it right on through sunrise, it will be evident to your naked eye in full daylight: a tiny white speck plainly evident against the blue daytime sky.

In a way, we could even regard Venus as this year's version of a "Christmas Star," glowing with stunning radiance ". . . in the east" like the biblical quote mentioned in St. Matthew.

What goes up, must come down

After reaching its high point in terms of morning visibility in mid-December, Venus will start a long, slow slide back toward the sun, rising about 1½ minutes later each morning from New Year's Day through late March. By then, Venus will be coming up as dawn is breaking, roughly 100 minutes before sunrise. Venus will continue to get gradually lower and rise progressively later during the spring and by late June it will be coming up less than an hour before sunrise, ultimately vanishing into the bright dawn twilight by July. Venus will then go on a "summer sabbatical" of sorts and will not reappear again until about this time next year when it will begin a very fine evening apparition.

So, if any of your friends or relatives remark to you that they saw a "strange UFO" on the way to work or school recently, you now can set them straight.

It's not E.T. It's only Venus.

   <title>Jaký byl listopad 1986: Hořely fabriky, Waldemar Matuška přišel o titul</title>
   <link>https://www.denik.cz/historie/jaky-byl-listopad-1986-horely-fabriky-waldemar-matuska-prisel-o-titul/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed-vse&utm_campaign=ceskolipsky.denik.cz&utm_content=historie</link>
   <description>Zase přišel ten čas, kdy se říjen slavil v listopadu – samozřejmě ten Velký. Krkonoše ohlásily první opravdovou bílou nadílku a tamní horská služba se radovala, že dostala tři nové sněžné skútry. A že se ochlazovalo, určitě někomu přišla vhod zpráva o tom, že brandýský Kovopodnik inovoval a víc než zdvojnásobil pětačtyřicetimilimetrovou izolaci maringotek, které monopolně vyráběl. Republiku potrápily mlhy – a nejen ji; taky západoněmeckého pilota, který po ztrátě orientace omylem přeletěl hranici a nouzově přistál u Holušic na Strakonicku.</description>

]]> Okresní kolo ČEPS Cupu – florbal 1. stupeň základních škol (kluci) 2026/2027 https://www.vybezek.eu/296441-okresni-kolo-ceps-cupu-florbal-1-stupen-zakladnich-skol-kluci-2026-2027/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 09:35:41 +0000 https://www.vybezek.eu/?p=296441 Ve středu 4. listopadu 2026 se ve Varnsdorfu ve sportovní hale hrál florbal, proběhlo okresní kolo ČEPS Cupu Děčín-Šluknovsko pro 1. stupeň základních škol (kluci).

Ve středu 4. listopadu 2026 se ve sportovní hale ve Varnsdorfu uskutečnilo okresní kolo florbalového turnaje ČEPS Cupu, určeného pro žáky 1.–5. tříd základních škol.

Turnaj se hrál systémem 3 + 1. Každý tým se utkal s každým soupeřem dvoukolově, přičemž jedno utkání trvalo 2 × 8 minut. Na turnaji se představily tři týmy – ZŠ Východní, Centrum dětí a mládeže Česká Kamenice a naše škola. Každý tým tak odehrál celkem čtyři utkání. Vítězný tým turnaje postoupí do krajského finále.

Hned v úvodním utkání nás čekal nejtěžší soupeř, domácí ZŠ Východní. Po velmi vyrovnaném a bojovném průběhu jsme dokázali zvítězit těsným výsledkem 4:3. Druhý zápas proti soupeři z České Kamenice jsme zvládli výborně a po přesvědčivém výkonu jsme zvítězili 6:2. Ve druhém kole jsme se znovu utkali se ZŠ Východní. Tentokrát nám soupeř porážku oplatil a po dramatickém průběhu jsme prohráli nejtěsnějším rozdílem 2:3. Jelikož i ZŠ Východní zvítězila nad Českou Kamenicí, bylo před závěrečným utkáním jasné, že o vítězi turnaje rozhodne počet vstřelených branek proti tomuto soupeři.

Do závěrečného utkání jsme proto nastoupili s jasnou taktikou – vstřelit co nejvíce branek. Po většinu turnaje nás v brance skvěle držel Adam Reichert, který několika výbornými zákroky podržel tým v nejtěžších chvílích. Pro rozhodující utkání jsme však zvolili odvážný taktický tah. Adama jsme přesunuli z branky do pole, protože sehraná trojice Adam Reichert, Hugo Bláha a Dominik Košín měla za úkol nastřílet co nejvíce gólů. Tento plán dokonale vyšel. Našemu týmu se podařilo zvítězit vysokým rozdílem a vstřelit soupeři 13 branek, tedy o tři více, než dokázala ZŠ Východní. Díky lepšímu skóre jsme se stali vítězi okresního kola a vybojovali si zasloužený postup do krajského finále.

Velkou pochvalu si zaslouží celý tým za bojovnost, nasazení a kolektivní výkon.
